title: Palms (Matthew 21:1–11)
hook: he rides in on a donkey and the crowd throws coats on the road

segments.voice: Last week ended at Lazarus's tomb, and the line Jesus wept. Did you let yourself grieve? Day fifty-seven. Now the road reaches Jerusalem. This is Holy Week.

Picture a parade. Presidents arrive in armored cars. Conquering generals in Rome rode in chariots, and kings entered cities on war horses. Everybody could see the power. Now it's springtime, just before Passover, and Jerusalem is packed with pilgrims. Jesus sends two disciples to a village on the Mount of Olives to fetch something for his entrance. Not a horse. A donkey, and her colt. They throw their cloaks over them and he sits on them. And the crowd goes wild. They spread their coats on the road in front of him. They cut branches from the trees and lay them down. And they shout one word, over and over. Today's word is what they shouted.
screen: `KINGS RIDE WAR HORSES.` → `HE SENDS FOR A DONKEY.` → `COATS AND BRANCHES ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's what the crowds cried, going before him and following, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, from a line in Psalm one hundred eighteen: hoshia na. Save, please. Save us now. It began as a cry for help, and over time it became a shout of praise, like a cheer. Both meanings are in the air that day: help us, and hooray. And the donkey is not an accident. Matthew says it happened to fulfill the prophet Zechariah: "Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass." A king, but a meek one. A king who comes in peace, not on a war horse. The whole city is stirred up, Matthew says, asking: who is this? And the crowds answer: this is Jesus the prophet, from Nazareth of Galilee. The Church relives this day every year on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week. Palms are blessed, and people carry them in procession into the church. Then, in the same Mass, the whole Passion is read, and the mood turns. The crowd's hosanna and the cross are held together on one day. Many Catholics take their blessed palms home, tuck them behind a crucifix, and bring them back the next year, when old palms are burned to make the ashes for Ash Wednesday. And every Mass, all year, Catholics sing this crowd's words in the Holy, Holy, Holy: hosanna in the highest.
screen: `HOSANNA — SAVE US, PLEASE.` · `A CRY FOR HELP BECOMES A CHEER.` · `A KING, MEEK, ON A DONKEY.` · `PALMS BLESSED, THEN BURNED FOR ASHES.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wave one small welcome today. Settle and breathe. Think about who is arriving in your day. A child coming home from school. A coworker walking in late. A neighbor, a guest, a stranger at the door. Most arrivals get a glance, or nothing. Choose one person, and picture giving them a real welcome: eyes up, a smile, their name. Not a parade. Just a coat on the road. If you pray, you can say the crowd's word, hosanna, as praise or as a cry for help. The bell holds the time.
Hosanna. From Hebrew: save us, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung at every Mass. Today's word.
Your line: a king on a donkey. Today, notice where power could show off, and choose the gentle way instead. Day fifty-seven.

howItsDone: On Palm Sunday Catholics receive blessed palms, walk in procession, and hear the Passion read; many keep the palms at home until they are burned for the next Ash Wednesday, and every Mass sings hosanna in the Sanctus.

fork.setup: you're about to enter the capital city at the height of the festival, and everyone expects a king. what do you ride?
options: a war horse, so the city sees your power.
nothing. you slip in quietly on foot.
fork.reveal: a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah: “Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass.”

original.note: Hebrew: save, please. From Psalm 118:25; in Greek it became hōsanna.

trapdoor: what you thought: hosanna is a happy church word.
what it means: a crowd crying save us! to a king who rides in on a donkey, meek, not on a war horse.
what a scholar hears: hoshia na, from Psalm 118:25, a plea that turned into praise. Matthew reads the donkey through Zechariah 9:9.
